Body.raw:
WHY
Teach programming to a gifted ~12-year-old using concrete visuals, not abstract-first syntax drills. imgcomp is the visual bedrock: lessons become rectangles on a canvas, sorting animations, interactive markup -- whatever makes the idea tangible. Pedagogy research leads; lesson topics (canvas shapes, animated sort, etc.) are background examples, not the product.

GOAL
Design and eventually build a ductile, responsive REPL layered on imgcomp so the learner can type, see, tweak, and feel immediate feedback. With caching (and related compositing work), target ~30fps for live preview / animation loops so interaction stays fluid.

OUT OF SCOPE (for now)
Full curriculum writing, classroom multi-student tooling, non-imgcomp graphics backends. Prefer evolving lessons on top of this REPL once the teaching model and feedback loop are clear.

CONSTRAINTS
- Center-based imgcomp scene graph (Shape / wrappers / SDF / NaiveCompositor) stays the render substrate.
- Stay ASCII-clean in human-readable project prose.
- Research first: how gifted middle-schoolers learn to code well; what REPL affordances matter (error warmth, undo, live binding of names to drawn objects, small steps).

PRODUCT DECISIONS (descoped at merge to master)
Learner language surface, host UX (Tk vs PNG), and lesson-module coupling were left open; spike ships Python-exec v0 + headless layer cache. Follow-ons may lock those without reopening pedagogy research.

Host/language product locks were descoped at merge; follow-ons can choose Tk vs PNG and Python-subset details later. Scope is utils/imgcomp.
